facts.text: The varied sittella is a small songbird native to Australia, also known as the Australian nuthatch, orange-winged sittella and the barkpecker.
facts.quote: About 10–11 cm long, it is also known as the Australian nuthatch, orange-winged sittella and the barkpecker.

facts.text: Its wings are black with a broad white or cinnamon bar, and its dark orange eye is ringed with orange-yellow.
facts.quote: Its wings are black, with a broad bar in either white or cinnamon. The iris is dark orange, and the eye-ring, legs and feet are orange-yellow.

facts.text: The sittella's crown and head can be white, grey or black depending on where it lives.
facts.quote: Its crown and head can be white, grey or black, and its body is either whitish or grey often streaked with black and grey.

facts.text: Flocks forage in trees of all heights, often descending erratically down trunks in a nuthatch-like fashion.
facts.quote: Flocks of the birds forage in trees of all heights, often descending erratically down the trunks in a rather nuthatch-like fashion.

facts.text: The sittella eats spiders and insects, usually prised from beneath the bark.
facts.quote: Their diet consists of spiders and insects, usually prised from beneath the bark.

facts.text: Its calls are a thin, high-pitched chwit that becomes a louder metallic tchweit-tchweit-tchweit as birds call back and forth.
facts.quote: Calls are a thin, high-pitched chwit becoming the louder, metallic tchweit-tchweit-tchweit of many birds combining in a constant call-and-response as they move towards another tree.

facts.text: In spring and summer, larger flocks break up into smaller breeding flocks that include a breeding pair and unmated adults from the previous season.
facts.quote: larger flocks break up into smaller breeding flocks, typically composed of a breeding pair, along with several unmated adults and immatures from the previous season.

facts.text: The cone-shaped nest, made of bark, fibres and spider-webs, is placed 5 to 25 m above ground on a branch.
facts.quote: The nest is cone-shaped, made of bark, fibres and spider-webs, and placed 5 to 25 m above ground in the fork of a branch or on an exposed limb.

facts.text: The female incubates a clutch of two or three blue-spotted white eggs for 18 to 20 days.
facts.quote: A clutch of two or three blue-spotted, white eggs, measuring 17 mm × 13 mm (0.7 in × 0.5 in), is incubated by the female for 18 to 20 days.
